results.title: Matching in a hypergraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a hypergraph on a vertex set $V$ whose edges form a set $E$ of finite subsets of $V$, a set $M$ is a matching when $M \subseteq E$ and any two distinct members of $M$ are disjoint.

results.title: Strongly maximal matching
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a hypergraph with edge set $E$, a set $M$ is a strongly maximal matching (Aharoni) when $M$ is a matching of $E$ and every matching $M'$ of $E$ satisfies $|M' \setminus M| \le |M \setminus M'|$, comparing the cardinalities as cardinal numbers.

results.title: Strongly maximal matchings in hypergraphs with bounded edges
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every vertex set $V$ and every set $E$ of finite subsets of $V$ such that some natural number $k$ bounds the number of elements of every edge in $E$, the hypergraph with edge set $E$ has a strongly maximal matching.

results.title: Bounded edge size does not guarantee a strongly maximal matching
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are a vertex set $V$, a set $E$ of finite subsets of $V$ and a natural number $k$ such that every edge in $E$ has at most $k$ elements, but the hypergraph with edge set $E$ has no strongly maximal matching.

results.title: Vertex cover of a hypergraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a set of finite subsets of a type $V$, the edges of a hypergraph. A set $X \subseteq V$ is a (vertex) cover of $E$ if it meets every edge: every $e \in E$ contains some $v \in X$.

results.title: Strongly minimal cover
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a set of finite subsets of a type $V$, the edges of a hypergraph. A set $X \subseteq V$ is a strongly minimal cover of $E$ (Aharoni) if $X$ is a cover of $E$, that is, it meets every edge in $E$, and $|X \setminus X'| \le |X' \setminus X|$, as cardinals, for every cover $X'$ of $E$.

results.title: Aharoni's strongly minimal cover conjecture
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every type $V$, every set $E$ of finite subsets of $V$ (the edges of a hypergraph, possibly infinitely many) and every natural number $k$ such that each edge in $E$ is nonempty and has at most $k$ elements, the hypergraph with edge set $E$ has a strongly minimal cover.

results.title: Domino (Post correspondence problem)
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A domino over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a pair $(t, b)$ of words over $\alpha$: its top word $t$ and its bottom word $b$.

results.title: Top word of a sequence of dominoes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequence of dominoes $(t_1, b_1), \ldots, (t_n, b_n)$, its top word is the concatenation $t_1 t_2 \cdots t_n$ of their top words; the empty sequence has the empty top word.

results.title: Bottom word of a domino sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequence $s = d_1, \dots, d_k$ of dominoes, the bottom word of $s$ is the concatenation $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_k$, where $b_i$ is the bottom word of $d_i$.

results.title: PCP solution
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be a finite list of dominoes. A solution of $P$ is a nonempty sequence $d_1, \dots, d_k$ of dominoes, each occurring in $P$ (repetitions allowed), such that the concatenation of the top words of $d_1, \dots, d_k$ equals the concatenation of their bottom words.

results.title: The Post correspondence problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes is a solvable instance of the Post correspondence problem when it has a PCP solution: a nonempty sequence of dominoes from $P$, repetitions allowed, whose top words and bottom words concatenate to the same word.

results.title: The modified Post correspondence problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes has an MPCP solution when $P$ is nonempty and some PCP solution of $P$ starts with the first domino of $P$.

results.title: Instances with nonempty words
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $P$ of dominoes has nonempty words when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top word and a nonempty bottom word.

results.title: The extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$, the extended alphabet consists of the letters of $\alpha$ together with two new symbols: the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$.

results.title: The alphabet inside the extended alphabet
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Each letter $a$ of the alphabet $\alpha$ is regarded as a symbol of the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction, which consists of the letters of $\alpha$, the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$.

results.title: The star symbol
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The star $\star$ is the new symbol of the extended alphabet that is neither a letter of $\alpha$ nor the end marker $\diamond$.

results.title: End marker
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The end marker $\diamond$ is the symbol of the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction that is neither a letter of $\alpha$ nor the star $\star$.

results.title: A star before every letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\star$ be the star of the extended alphabet. For a word $u = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\alpha$, the word $\star u$ over the extended alphabet is $\star a_1 \star a_2 \cdots \star a_n$, obtained by putting a star before every letter of $u$; the empty word gives the empty word.

results.title: A star after every letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\star$ be the star of the extended alphabet. For a word $u = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\alpha$, the word $u\star$ over the extended alphabet is $a_1 \star a_2 \star \cdots a_n \star$, obtained by putting a star after every letter of $u$; the empty word gives the empty word.

results.title: Erasing stars and end markers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $w$ over the extended alphabet of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction, this is the word over $\alpha$ obtained from $w$ by deleting every star $\star$ and every end marker $\diamond$, keeping the letters of $\alpha$ in their order.

results.title: Starred image of a domino
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $u$ over $\alpha$, write $\star u$ for the word over the extended alphabet obtained by putting a star $\star$ before every letter of $u$, and $u\star$ for the word obtained by putting a star after every letter. A domino $(t, b)$ over $\alpha$ is sent to the domino $(\star t, b\star)$ over the extended alphabet.

results.title: The start domino of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a domino $(t, b)$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, its start domino is the domino $(\star t, \star b \star)$ over the extended alphabet, where $\star t$ puts the star $\star$ before every letter of $t$ and $b \star$ puts a star after every letter of $b$, so that the bottom word gets one extra star in front.

results.title: End domino of the MPCP-to-PCP reduction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Over the alphabet $\alpha$ extended with the star $\star$ and the end marker $\diamond$, the end domino is $(\star\diamond, \diamond)$: its top word is $\star$ followed by $\diamond$, and its bottom word is $\diamond$.

results.title: The reduction from MPCP to PCP
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\star$ for the star and $\diamond$ for the end marker of the extended alphabet; for a word $u$ over $\alpha$, $\star u$ puts a star before every letter of $u$ and $u \star$ puts a star after every letter of $u$. The empty list of dominoes is sent to the empty list. A list $P = [d_0, d_1, \ldots, d_n]$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, with $d_0 = (t_0, b_0)$, is sent to the following list of dominoes over the…

results.title: Erasing the markers from a domino
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a domino $(t, b)$ over the extended alphabet, its unmapping is the domino over $\alpha$ obtained by deleting every star $\star$ and every end marker $\diamond$ from both $t$ and $b$, keeping the letters of $\alpha$ in order.

results.title: An MPCP solution gives a PCP solution of the reduced instance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a list $P$ of dominoes has an MPCP solution, then the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP has a PCP solution.

results.title: On instances with nonempty words, a PCP solution of the reduced instance gives an MPCP solution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On instances with nonempty words, a PCP solution of the reduced instance gives an MPCP solution. Let $P$ be a list of dominoes in which every domino has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom. If the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP has a PCP solution, then $P$ has an MPCP solution.

results.title: MPCP reduces to PCP on instances with nonempty words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a list of dominoes over an alphabet $\alpha$ in which every domino has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom. Then $P$ has an MPCP solution if and only if the image of $P$ under the reduction from MPCP to PCP, an instance over $\alpha$ extended with a star and an end marker, has a PCP solution.

results.title: Boolean test for nonempty words
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $P$ of dominoes, this Boolean test returns true exactly when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom.

results.title: The total reduction from MPCP to PCP
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $P$ of dominoes, the total reduction sends $P$ to its image under the reduction from MPCP to PCP when every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom, and to the empty instance, which has no PCP solution, otherwise.

results.title: The nonempty-words test is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive coding, the Boolean test of whether every domino of a list over $\alpha$ has a nonempty top and a nonempty bottom is a primitive recursive function of the list.

results.title: MPCP many-one reduces to PCP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding, and let $\alpha'$ be $\alpha$ extended with two new symbols, the star and the end marker. There is a computable function $f$ from finite lists of dominoes over $\alpha$ to finite lists of dominoes over $\alpha'$ such that, for every list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, $f(P)$ has a PCP solution if and only if both every domino of $P$ has a nonempty top…

results.title: Boolean check for PCP solutions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding and decidable equality, and let $P$ and $s$ be lists of dominoes over $\alpha$. The Boolean solution check of $s$ for $P$ is true exactly when $s$ is nonempty, every domino of $s$ occurs in $P$, and the top word of $s$ equals the bottom word of $s$, and it is false otherwise.

results.title: PCP is recursively enumerable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive coding, the set of lists of dominoes over $\alpha$ that have a PCP solution is recursively enumerable.

results.title: PCP is Turing-recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, there is a multi-stack Turing machine that, started on the binary encoding of a list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, halts exactly when $P$ has a PCP solution.

results.title: Total length of dominoes that are at least as long on top
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. Let $s$ be a finite sequence of dominoes over an alphabet. If every domino $(t, b)$ in $s$ satisfies $|b| \le |t|$, then the concatenation of the bottom words of $s$ is no longer than the concatenation of the top words of $s$.

results.title: Total length of dominoes that are strictly longer on top
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. Let $s$ be a nonempty finite sequence of dominoes over an alphabet. If every domino $(t, b)$ in $s$ satisfies $|b| < |t|$, then the concatenation of the bottom words of $s$ is strictly shorter than the concatenation of the top words of $s$.

results.title: Swapping top and bottom
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of dominoes, the swapped sequence is obtained from $s$ by exchanging the top and bottom word of every domino: each $(t, b)$ becomes $(b, t)$, and the order of the dominoes is unchanged.

results.title: The unary PCP criterion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter, and write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. A finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$ has a PCP solution if and only if either some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| = |b|$, or some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| < |b|$ and some domino $(t', b')$ in $P$ has $|b'| < |t'|$.

results.title: The unary PCP test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter, and write $|w|$ for the length of a word $w$. For a finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, the unary test of $P$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| = |b|$, or some domino $(t, b)$ in $P$ has $|t| < |b|$ and some domino $(t', b')$ in $P$ has $|b'| < |t'|$.

results.title: PCP over a one-letter alphabet is decidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter whose elements have a computable encoding. Then the Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is a computable predicate: some computable function decides, for every finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether $P$ has a PCP solution.

results.title: Unary PCP is decidable by a multi-stack machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one letter whose elements have a computable encoding. Then the Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine: some multi-stack Turing machine decides, for every finite list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether $P$ has a PCP solution.

results.title: Symbols of the rewriting system of a single-tape machine
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and a set of states $\Lambda$, the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine are a tape symbol $a$ for each $a \in \Gamma$, a state symbol $q$ for each $q \in \Lambda$, the left end marker $\vdash$, the right end marker $\dashv$ and the halting symbol $H$.

results.title: Control symbols
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A symbol of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape Turing machine is a control symbol if it is a state symbol or the halting symbol $H$; tape symbols and the end markers $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are not control symbols.

results.title: Unique splitting at a marked letter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a property of the elements of a type $\alpha$, let $A$ and $B$ be lists over $\alpha$ none of whose elements satisfy $P$, and let $y \in \alpha$. If $C$ and $D$ are lists over $\alpha$ and $x \in \alpha$ satisfies $P$ with $C\,x\,D = A\,y\,B$ (concatenation), then $C = A$, $x = y$ and $D = B$.

results.title: Splitting a rewrite site at its control symbol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $u$, $v$, $p$, $s$ be words over the symbols of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine, and let $x$ and $y$ be symbols. If no symbol of $A$ or of $B$ is a control symbol (a state symbol or the halting symbol), $x$ is a control symbol, and $u\,p\,x\,s\,v = A\,y\,B$, then $u\,p = A$, $x = y$ and $s\,v = B$.

results.title: The word of a configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a state $q$, a tape symbol $h$ and words $L$, $R$ of tape symbols, the word of the configuration in state $q$ with head symbol $h$, left part $L$ (in reading order, from left to right) and right part $R$ is $\vdash L\,q\,h\,R \dashv$, where $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are the end markers.

results.title: The halting word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The halting word is the word $\vdash H \dashv$ made of the left end marker, the halting symbol and the right end marker. It is the target word of the rewriting simulation of a single-tape machine.

results.title: Words spelling a configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A word $w$ spells a configuration $c$ of a single-tape Turing machine if there are a state $q$, a tape symbol $h$ and words $L$, $R$ of tape symbols such that $c$ is in state $q$, its head reads $h$, its tape reads $L$ immediately to the left of the head and $R$ immediately to the right of it, with blanks beyond, and $w = \vdash L\,q\,h\,R \dashv$.

results.title: The start word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an input $l$ of tape symbols, the start word is $\vdash q_0\, h\, R \dashv$, where $\vdash$ and $\dashv$ are the left and right end markers, $q_0$ is the default state, $h$ is the first symbol of $l$ (the default tape symbol if $l$ is empty) and $R$ is the rest of $l$. It spells the configuration in state $q_0$ with head symbol $h$, empty left part and right part $R$.

results.title: Erasing rules
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite tape alphabet $\Gamma$, let $H$ be the halting symbol of the rewriting system simulating a single-tape machine with tape alphabet $\Gamma$. The erasing rules are the rewriting rules $c\,H \to H$ and $H\,c \to H$ for every tape symbol $c \in \Gamma$: the halting symbol deletes the tape symbol on either side of it.

results.title: The rewriting system simulating a Turing machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and write $H$ for the halting symbol. The rewriting system simulating $M$ is the finite list of rules consisting of the rules for every state $q$ reading every tape symbol $a$, followed by the erasing rules $c\,H \to H$ and $H\,c \to H$ for every tape symbol $c$.

results.title: Boolean test for control symbols
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Number of control symbols
results.caption: Definition

results.title: A word with one control symbol splits at it

results.title: Rewriting at a state symbol

results.title: Reversible semigroup of transition matrices
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A family of transition matrices `P t`, indexed by branch length, is a reversible semigroup for the distribution `π`: it satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation and detailed balance `π a P t a b = π b P t b a`. With rows summing to `1`, detailed balance makes `π` stationary; the pulley principle uses only the two equations below.

results.title: Partial likelihoods are invariant under swapping subtrees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Swapping the two subtrees of a node does not change its partial likelihoods; with `likelihood_node_comm` this lets the rerooting move `likelihood_reroot` reach either child.

results.title: Likelihood is invariant under swapping root subtrees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Swapping the two subtrees of the root does not change the likelihood.

results.title: The root can be pushed to the end of its edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With the root on the edge between the subtrees `l` and `r`, at distances `s` and `t`, the likelihood is that of the root placed at the root of `l`, with `r` at distance `s + t`.

results.title: Pulley principle, sliding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Moving the root along its edge does not change the likelihood (Felsenstein 1981).

results.title: Pulley principle, rerooting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the root sit on the edge between an internal vertex `x` (at distance `s₁`) and the subtree `C` (at distance `s₂`), where `x` has the subtrees `A` and `B` at distances `a` and `b`. Moving the root to the edge between `x` and `A`, at distance `u₁` from `A` and `u₂` from `x` with `u₁ + u₂ = a`, gives the same likelihood: the unrooted tree and its edge lengths are unchanged (Felsenstein 1981).

results.title: Reversible continuous-time models give reversible semigroups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A reversible continuous-time model gives a reversible semigroup: if `π` is in detailed balance with the generator `Q`, the transition functions `exp (t • Q)` form a reversible semigroup for `π`.

results.title: LogDet (paralinear) distance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The LogDet (paralinear) distance of a joint distribution matrix `F` (`F i j = ℙ(X = i, Y = j)`): `-log |det F| + (log det Π_X + log det Π_Y) / 2`, where the diagonal marginal matrices have determinants `∏ i, ∑ j, F i j` and `∏ j, ∑ i, F i j`. It is a distance only when `det F ≠ 0` and the marginals are positive; otherwise the value is Lean's totalized logarithm (`log 0 = 0`).

results.title: LogDet distance of a vertex to itself is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The distance of a vertex to itself is `0`: the joint distribution of `X` with itself is the diagonal matrix of its (positive) marginal.

results.title: Nonsingular transition matrices preserve positive distributions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under a nonnegative, nonsingular transition matrix, a positive distribution stays positive: every column of `M` has a positive entry. This puts the LogDet logarithms in their domain.

results.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Additivity of the LogDet distance at a separating vertex (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al. 1994; Lake 1994). Let `Y` have distribution `p` (positive) and let `X` and `Z` be conditionally independent given `Y`, with transition matrices `M` (from `Y` to `X`) and `N` (from `Y` to `Z`) whose rows sum to `1` and whose determinants are nonzero. The joint distribution matrices are `F_XY = Mᵀ Π_Y`, `F_YZ = Π_Y N` and…

results.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a chain, one step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Markov chain `X → Y → Z` with `X` distributed as `p` (positive), transition matrices `A` (nonnegative) and `B` with unit row sums and nonzero determinants, `d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z)`, where `F_XZ = Π_X A B`, `F_XY = Π_X A` and `F_YZ = Π_Y B` with `Y` distributed as `p A`.

results.title: Product of transition matrices along a path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The product `M 0 * M 1 * ⋯ * M (n - 1)` of the transition matrices along the first `n` edges of a path.

results.title: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Additivity of the LogDet distance along a path (Steel 1994; Lockhart et al. 1994): for a Markov chain `v₀ → v₁ → ⋯ → v_n` along a path, with positive initial distribution `p` and nonnegative nonsingular transition matrices `M i` with unit row sums, the LogDet distance between the ends is the sum of the distances of consecutive vertices. results.title: Symmetric two-state model on a branch
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The symmetric two-state model on one branch: the state changes with probability `p`. As a model, `0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2`.

results.title: Four-taxon quartet tree model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The quartet `((A, B), (C, D))` on the taxa `0 = A`, `1 = B`, `2 = C`, `3 = D`, with change probabilities `pA, pB, pC, pD` on the pendant edges and `pI` on the internal edge. The root sits at the `AB` end of the internal edge (the edge to the `AB` cherry vertex has change probability `0`); by the pulley principle its position does not matter.

results.title: Leaf weights of a site pattern
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The leaf weights of a site pattern `σ`: the indicator of the observed state.

results.title: Probability of a site pattern on a quartet
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The probability of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet, with the uniform root distribution (the stationary distribution of the symmetric model).

results.title: Site pattern probabilities sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The pattern probabilities sum to `1`, for all parameters.

results.title: Nonnegativity of site pattern probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The pattern probabilities are nonnegative for change probabilities in `[0, 1]`.

results.title: Site pattern supporting a split
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The site pattern `σ` supports the split `{a, b} | {c, d}`: `a, b` agree, `c, d` agree, and the two pairs differ (a parsimony-informative pattern for that split).

results.title: Expected frequency of patterns supporting a split
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The expected frequency of the patterns supporting the split `{a, b} | {c, d}`.

results.title: Felsenstein (1978), the exact comparison
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With change probability `P` on the long non-sister branches to `A` and `C` and `Q` on the other three branches, the expected frequency of patterns supporting the wrong split `AC | BD` exceeds that of the true split `AB | CD` by `(1 - 2 Q) (P ^ 2 - Q (1 - Q))`, for all real `P, Q`. This is Felsenstein's equations (16)–(17) (his four-species model has equal probabilities of change `0 → 1` and reversion `1 → 0`).

results.title: Wrong split against third split frequency difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The wrong split `AC | BD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected frequencies is `(1 - 2 Q) (P - Q) ^ 2`.

results.title: True split against third split frequency difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The true split `AB | CD` against the third split `AD | BC`: the difference of expected frequencies is `Q (1 - 2 Q) (1 - 2 P)`.

results.title: Rooted quartet with unit costs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The rooted quartet `((a, b), (c, d))` with unit costs, for Fitch's algorithm.

results.title: Fitch parsimony score on a quartet
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Fitch parsimony score of the site pattern `σ` on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`; it is the small-parsimony score by `Parsimony.fitch_score_eq`.

results.title: Difference of parsimony scores of two quartets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On four taxa, the parsimony scores of two quartets differ only on informative patterns: the score on `AB | CD` minus the score on `AC | BD` is `1` on patterns supporting `AC | BD`, `-1` on patterns supporting `AB | CD`, and `0` otherwise; likewise for `AD | BC`.

results.title: Expected Fitch parsimony score on a quartet
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The expected Fitch parsimony score of one site on the quartet `((a, b), (c, d))`.

results.title: The Felsenstein zone
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Felsenstein zone (Felsenstein 1978): if `0 ≤ Q < 1/2` and `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, the wrong quartet `AC | BD` has strictly smaller expected parsimony score per site than both the true quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`. The statement is algebraic in `P`; the model has `0 ≤ P ≤ 1/2`.

results.title: Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Parsimony is inconsistent in the Felsenstein zone (Felsenstein 1978): if the sites `σ i` are pairwise independent and identically distributed with the pattern distribution of the quartet, and `0 ≤ Q < 1/2`, `P ^ 2 > Q (1 - Q)`, then almost surely, for all long enough alignments, the wrong quartet `AC | BD` has a strictly smaller total Fitch score than the true quartet `AB | CD` and the third quartet `AD | BC`.

results.title: Chapman–Kolmogorov along a path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The JC transition matrix along a path is the transition matrix of the total length.

results.title: JC-corrected distances are path lengths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: JC-corrected distances are path lengths (Jukes & Cantor 1969): the JC distance of the probability that the two ends of a path differ is `μ` times the total branch length.

results.title: Empirical p-distance

results.summary: The empirical p-distance of the taxa `x, y` over the first `n` sites of the alignment `seq` (`seq i x` is the base of taxon `x` at site `i`): the proportion of sites where they differ.

results.title: Strong law for the p-distances
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For pairwise independent, identically distributed sites, the empirical p-distance of every pair of taxa converges almost surely to the probability that the two taxa differ at a site.

results.summary: Let `d` be the path-length metric of a binary phylogenetic `X`-tree `(G, ι)` with positive edge lengths `w` whose internal edges (no taxon at either end) have length at least `m`.
